units.spoken: RL Method Families: Values, Policies and Models
Learn how good things are, what to do, or how the world works. Which kind of learning each family of methods does, and when to reach for it.

A learner can get better from rewards in more than one way. It can learn how good each situation is, learn what to do directly, or learn how the world responds and plan with that. Which of these should a method learn, and what goes wrong with each?

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad. Here the agent is a warehouse robot that must reach its charging dock. It starts in one bottom corner and the dock sits in the other.
The floor is a grid of cells, one per place the robot can stand. It knows only which cell it stands in, not where each move leads or what it costs.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends. The ledge is the strip of floor between the start and the dock. Reaching the dock can take many moves.

Each move's reward is minus the battery it uses, so the best total is the one closest to zero. Every move costs a little battery; stepping onto the ledge costs a lot and puts the robot back at the start; only reaching the dock ends the episode. The cheapest way to the dock is the shortest path that never steps onto the ledge.

Take a look at this figure. The floor looks simple, with a start at one end and a dock at the other, yet the cheap route is not the short one. The ledge sits between them, and crossing it costs more battery than walking around it, so the robot that chases the shortest path pays the most. That gap between short and cheap is the whole problem, and every method that follows learns the same lesson, that a good route spends the least, not the one that looks nearest.

Figure 1 shows the floor the robot learns on. The short way is not the cheap way: a robot one cell from the dock with the ledge in between pays a lot to cross it, so the cheap way goes around. This one floor is the whole problem every method on the page learns on, so the rest of the page is three ways of learning on it.
Section one, What an agent can learn
RL, short for reinforcement learning, is learning which moves to make from rewards rather than from labelled answers. Nobody shows the robot the route to the dock; it finds one only by trying steps.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. Next to the dock little battery is left to spend, so the return there is the best on the floor.

A state's value is the return the agent expects from that state. A move's value, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes that move in that state and plays on from there. A robot that starts far from the dock passes many cells before it reaches it, while one that starts beside it is nearly there.

Every method on this page wants the same thing: the cheapest route to the dock, the most return. The three families are three different things a learner can store between steps: scores for its moves, chances for its moves, or guesses about the world. Which one a method stores decides how it acts and where it is used.
Values: learn how good each move is

A value method keeps a score for every move in every cell, the return the robot expects if it makes that move. Each real step nudges the score of the move just taken toward what followed, and the robot acts by picking the best-scored move in its cell.

What breaks is the untried move. A move never tried has no score worth trusting, so the robot must keep trying moves, and scores built on guesses can climb higher than the robot really earns. States that never repeat cannot be listed in a table, so a network must compute the scores, which is Deep Q-Networks (DQN). Double DQN fixes the climbing scores with a second network that scores the move the first one picked.

Value methods are used now where no two readings of the world match, so a network computes the scores. A reading is what the robot senses of its state. Where every step scores almost the same, as in a cell far from the dock, learning how good the spot is once beats scoring every step, which is Dueling DQN.
Policies: learn what to do

A policy method learns the chances themselves: in each cell it stores how likely each move is, and the robot acts by drawing a move from those chances. It learns by pushing up the chances of moves that turned out well and pushing down the ones that did not. In its simplest form it waits until the episode ends to know how a move turned out, which is REINFORCE. Actor-critic pairs the actor, the policy network that picks the moves, with the critic, a second network that judges each step at once, so the policy need not wait.

A policy is needed where the moves are not a short list. A robot arm sets turning forces, and scoring every possible force one by one is impossible, so the policy must output the amount directly. The same reason is why a language model is trained as a policy: its move is the next word piece, and there are far too many possible replies to score them one by one.

What breaks is one update moving the chances too far. A single stretch of play can wreck a policy that already worked, which is why PPO, short for Proximal Policy Optimization, caps how far one update can move the chances. The deterministic actor of DDPG, short for Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, outputs one set of turning forces, called torques, and needs outside noise to try anything new, while the stochastic actor of SAC, short for Soft Actor-Critic, draws its torques at random, most often near a centre.
Models: learn how the world works

A model method learns the world itself: for each cell and move it stores a guess about the next cell and the next reward, learned from real steps. It then practises on imagined steps, steps inside the model rather than in the real world, before spending a real step, like a chess player trying moves in their head.

A route tried in its head costs no battery, so the robot learns more from each real step. Imagined steps matter when real steps are slow or costly, as for a robot learning from camera images. Where no rules are given, the model itself must be learned from what the robot sees and the battery it spends, and planning runs on the learned rules.
What breaks is the guess. A model that never saw the ledge knows nothing about it, and plans built on wrong guesses go wrong. So the model must keep collecting real steps to correct itself.

What this picture is teaching is that one floor holds three kinds of knowledge at once, and early on they disagree. Each kind is learned from different steps and settles at its own speed, so the value picture can look settled while the policy still points the wrong way, and the model can guess a landing the robot has never tried. The three agree only when learning has settled, and that agreement is the sign the robot truly knows the floor.

The same floor holds three kinds of knowledge at once. In one look: the shade picture shows where the robot expects to earn, the arrow picture shows what it would do, and the dashed arrows show what it believes about the world. The three agree only when learning has settled.
Same goal, three routes
This table lines up the three families side by side. Find a family in the first column and read across to see what it stores, what it needs to act, what breaks, and where it is used now.

The families combine. Actor-critic is a policy plus a value judge, so the policy borrows the value family's tool to judge each step at once. A model-based method still needs a policy or scores to act, and Dyna replays imagined steps through the value update.
A model-free method learns scores or chances from real steps, with no model of the world. A model-based method also learns the world and practises inside it before acting for real.

Sample efficiency is how much an agent learns from each real step. Model error is where the model's guess differs from the real world, so plans built on it go wrong. A robot that only tried safe steps has a model that knows nothing about the ledge. The model's price is model error, and the value method's price is many real steps.

sections.section: 2 Values, policies and models as equations

units.spoken: Section two, Values, policies and models as equations

A network's weights are the numbers training adjusts; in this series value weights are written one way and policy weights another. On the floor, training changes the robot's numbers a little after every step it takes.

An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is. The sign marks an expected value. The robot's scores are such averages, learned from the steps it really takes.
Take the warehouse robot standing in a cell next to the ledge.

Equation 1. The rest of the page sorts methods into three families, and each family is judged by what it learns, so the page first names the three kinds of learning on the same robot and the same floor. A warehouse robot reaching its charging dock is the running example for the whole page.
Take a look at this equation. Three lines, one per family.

The policy average weights each future by how likely it is, so luck is priced in. The return from step t counts the battery still to spend, later moves counting less. The learned score for a cell and a move lives in the value weights, and approximately means training pulls the score toward it, not equal by definition.
Intuition. A score for each move says how good it is from here.
Example. Take the robot in the cell beside the ledge, eyeing the move toward the dock: the learned score for that move is the return it expects from the dock side, not from the ledge.

The policy gives each move a chance instead of scoring it. The chance of a move in a cell is one number per move in each cell, and the chances in one cell add to one, so some move is always picked. The chances live in the policy weights, and changing the weights changes the chances.
Intuition. A policy is a rule for choosing: in each cell it says how likely each move is. The policy writes that rule as chances.
Example. Take the robot beside the ledge: the policy gives the move toward the dock a high chance and the step onto the ledge a low one, so the robot usually walks on.

The world does not answer a move with one landing. The same move can land on the dock or slip onto the ledge, and each landing costs different battery, so the model writes its guess as chances over landings and rewards. Chances carry the odds the robot has seen, and planning with the odds beats planning on one guessed landing.
Intuition. A model guesses where a move lands and what it pays. The model writes that guess as chances.
Example. Take the robot beside the ledge stepping toward the dock: the model gives a high chance of landing on the dock and a small chance of slipping onto the ledge.

Take the robot standing in the cell next to the ledge, with the dock just past the ledge. The value line scores the move toward the dock by the return it expects from there, the policy line gives that move a high chance and the move onto the ledge a low one, and the model line gives the chance the move toward the dock lands the robot on the dock and the chance it lands on the ledge instead. Together the three lines say one thing: a value method scores each move, a policy method gives each move a chance, and a model method gives each landing and reward a chance.
The warehouse robot can learn any of the three from the same steps on the floor.

sections.section: 3 What each RL method learns and fixes

units.spoken: Section three, What each RL method learns and fixes

Section 1 gave you three families. This section walks the methods inside them. Each method exists because something breaks, or because the problem changes shape. Read each one in three lines: what it is, how it works, and why it works. They all chase the same end, the cheapest route to the dock.
Value methods
Q-Learning
Picture the robot with no map and no teacher, trying moves and remembering which paid off. A move toward the dock earns a high score; a step onto the ledge earns a low one.
How. Each step updates the score of the move just taken, toward the best score the next state offers.
When it works, the scores settle and the cheap route stands out. It is the simplest learner, the starting point for the rest.
SARSA (state, action, reward, state, action)

What. The same table, but scored for the moves the robot really plays, random ones included. Picture the robot taking a random step toward the ledge: the score it learns is for the move it really took.
Learn from the move really played, not the best move it could have played.
Why. Its route keeps away from the ledge, because it learns the cost of the random moves it takes. Learning from the moves really played is on-policy; learning from the best move is off-policy.
DQN
What. Some states never repeat, so no table can hold their scores. Picture the robot's readings: no two match, so a table can never be filled.
How. A network reads the state and outputs a score per move.
Why. The robot learns in a world that never repeats, which a table could never cover.
Double DQN
Picture the robot trusting its own guesses. Each score is a guess built on earlier guesses, and the highest guess is usually the luckiest one, not the best move.
How. A second network scores the move the first one picked, so the scores stop climbing.
When it works, the scores sit where the robot really earns, and the route it picks is the cheap one, because the scores no longer run high.
Dueling DQN
Picture the robot far from the dock, where every step costs the same and no move looks better than another. The spot is bad, not the step.
Split the score into how good the spot is, plus what the step adds.
When it works, the robot learns the floor faster: it knows a bad corner after one visit instead of trying every move out of it.
Policy methods
Policy gradient

Picture the robot learning the choice itself: in each cell it keeps a chance for every move, and the good moves get likelier. The trouble is the wait: it only learns how a move turned out when the episode ends.
Push up the chances of moves that turned out well.
When it works, the robot's choices sharpen: the good moves get likelier, and the policy itself is what it learned, with no scores in between.
Actor-critic
What. Waiting until the episode ends is slow. Picture the step onto the ledge: its cost is already clear, so there is no reason to wait for the episode to end.
How. A second network, the critic, judges each step at once, so the policy learns from every step.
When it works, the policy learns from each step as it happens.
PPO
Picture a policy that already works, then one big update shoves its chances too far and the good behaviour is gone.
Cap how far one update can move the chances, a cap called the clip, and learn from each stretch of play several times.
When it works, learning is steady: each update is a small step that keeps what works. It is used now for smooth moves in robot control and for training language models to write replies people prefer.
Continuous-action methods: DDPG and SAC
What. Some moves are amounts, not a short list. Picture a robot arm setting four turning forces, each from minus 1 to 1: scoring every force one by one is impossible.
How. The policy outputs the amount directly: DDPG one fixed set of forces, with outside noise to try anything new, and SAC forces drawn at random.
When it works, the arm moves smoothly instead of in jerks: the policy gives the amount, not a score for each one.
Model methods
Dyna
Picture the robot replaying a step in its head many times, learning from it each time, without spending battery.
Run the Q-learning update on imagined steps as well as real ones.
Why. Each real step teaches more, so the robot needs fewer real steps to learn.
Dreamer
What. Some robots learn from camera frames. Picture a robot learning to move by acting inside imagined experience, without touching the floor.
Learn a model of the world from what it sees, then act entirely inside imagined experience.
Why. The policy learns without spending real steps.
AlphaZero

What. Where the rules are known, the model can plan ahead instead of guessing. Picture the robot trying move sequences in its head before touching the floor, and learning from chess games against itself.
Plan ahead with the rules of chess, looking over move sequences, and learn from the games it plays against itself.
Why. The robot improves by playing itself, without human games or human examples.
MuZero

What. Where no rules are given, the model must learn the rules too. Picture a robot with no map of the floor, learning where the ledge is and what it costs from what it sees and the battery it spends.
Learn the rules inside the network, then plan ahead with the learned rules.
Why. The robot plans ahead even where nobody gave it the rules.
Several learners, one floor
Multi-agent methods
Picture two robots on one floor. Each one's steps change the world the other learns in, so the floor keeps changing as the other robot learns.
How. Each learner trains with a critic that sees what the other learners do, so each move is judged knowing the others' moves.
When it works, each learner's policy holds up against a moving opponent instead of a fixed floor.
Language-model methods

A language model starts as a predictor of the next word piece, or token. Given a question, it may carry on with more questions instead of answering. In RL terms, the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, the move is the next token, and the reward comes only when the reply ends.

Scoring every possible next word is impossible, so a policy method learns the chances directly. The clip works on chances alone, comparing the move's new chance with its old one, so it works for word pieces too.
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

Picture a predictor that only carries on: given words, it writes the next words, but it never answers a question, because answering was never its job. People cannot write a rule for a good answer; they can only compare two replies and say which they prefer.

How. RLHF takes three stages: training on replies people wrote, called supervised fine-tuning (SFT); training a reward model on people's comparisons; then reinforcement learning against it. A reward model is a language model with a one-number output, trained so the preferred reply scores higher. PPO moves the policy.
When it works, the model stops carrying on and starts answering: the reply it writes is the one people would have picked.
GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)
Picture the usual route's price: a second network, the critic, about as big as the model, trained alongside it. The critic is a whole second model to teach, just to judge the first one.

How. GRPO writes a group of answers to one question and lets them set their own bar, so no critic is needed. Where a program can check the answer, GRPO runs with an answer checker instead of a reward model.
When it works, the group does the critic's job for free: an answer that beats its siblings is a good answer, with no second model to train.
DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
Picture the usual route's slowness: it keeps writing fresh replies, scoring them, and updating, round after round. The loop is the bottleneck.

Train on fixed pairs of replies and never run the write, score, update loop, with no separate scorer. Use it on pairs where people picked the better reply. Where few people have marked replies as harmful, use Constitutional AI, which writes the labels from a written list of rules instead of from people's marks.
When it works, the policy learns from replies already written: no fresh writing, no loop, just the pairs.

The method is the answer to what your problem gives you, not a ranking of the families. A short list of moves takes a table of scores. Amounts or words take a policy. Costly real steps take a model. Several learners take one policy each, trained together.
This table is the lookup for the whole section. Find a method in the first column and read across to see what it learns and what it fixes. Read two rows together to compare two methods.

sections.section: 4 Values, policy and model on the same floor

units.spoken: Section four, Values, policy and model on the same floor

Take a look at this figure. One run, three views, and the three families learn at different speeds from the same steps. The model view is the revealing one early on, because a model must guess about moves it has never tried, and a guess with no evidence behind it is loose. As the run goes on the guesses sharpen, because each real step corrects them. The lesson is that a model is only as good as the steps it has seen.

Try switching to the Model view at the start of a run and pressing Play. Watch the model's guesses at the ledge edges: early on it calls untried edges safe, and as the run goes on the guesses sharpen. Watch how fast the guesses change once the robot tries the ledge edges for real.

Figure 2 shows the same floor three ways, so the three families can be compared on one run. Switch views on one run and compare how each family learns. Take the Model view at the start, when the robot has barely tried anything: its guesses are at their loosest, and as the run goes on they sharpen.

Here is the point of this figure. After the run every cell has been tried, so the shading is the robot's knowledge made visible. Knowledge is strongest where the return is nearly spent, beside the dock, because there the robot knows the way home in a few steps. Far away it stays pale, because those places are many steps from the dock and their value depends on everything in between, which the robot has not yet learned to price. It maps what the robot has learned, not the floor itself.

Figure 3 shows the values view after the run, when every floor cell has been tried. The shading is the robot's knowledge made visible: a cell beside the dock shaded strong blue says the robot knows the way home from there, and the pale cells far away say it has not yet learned how much those places cost.

What this figure is teaching is that a policy still forming does not trace one clean route. Each arrow is the move the robot would pick from that cell, and where the scores are still settling the arrows disagree, one pointing along the ledge where the cheap route goes around it. That disagreement is not a mistake in the picture, it is the learning itself, half done. A finished policy would point every cell toward the cheap way home, and this one is on its way there.

Figure 4 shows the policy view after the run, the move the robot would pick from every cell it has tried. The arrows do not trace one clean route, because the run is short and the scores are settling: a cell above the ledge may point along the ledge rather than around it, the route the robot has not yet learned. What the arrows show is a policy still forming, not a finished route.
Section five, Choosing a family
This table turns the choice around. Start from your situation, not from the methods. Find the question that matches your problem and read across to the method to reach for first.

Table 2 turns the choice around: start from your situation and it names the method to reach for first. Each row asks one question about your problem, and the second column names the method to start with. The questions run from the simplest floor to the hardest cases, so the first matching row is the place to begin. Take a robot that must stay safe while it still tries random moves: the table points to SARSA, which scores the moves it really plays.
Q-Learning is the place to start: if you kept a table with a score for every move in every cell, how would you fill it from experience?
